newsitem.title: USA: New-home sales ease in March but sizzle in first quarter.
newsitem.headline: New-home sales ease in March but sizzle in first quarter.

text.p: New home sales barely eased in March despite rising interest rates, the Commerce Department said Monday, setting a sizzling first-quarter pace that reflected strong economic momentum.

Nationwide sales were down 2.5 percent last month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 813,000 units from a steeply revised 1.1 percent gain in February to 834,000 units -- the strongest sales month since 857,000 in April 1986.
Previously, the department said sales had fallen by 0.7 percent in February to a rate of 811,000, instead of rising.

Analysts said the housing sector, which is especially sensitive to changes in interest rates, appeared to be at least leveling off but said it was not doing so fast enough to head off more interest-rate rises.

The government revised up its estimates of new home sales for every month from December through February. As a result, the first quarter's average monthly sales rate was 824,000 -- the hottest pace in more than 18 years since they were moving at an average 825,000 a month in the fourth quarter of 1978.

"Clearly, housing has misbehaved from the Fed's point of view," said economist David Seiders of the National Association of Home Builders. He noted Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan told Congress earlier this year that he anticipated some easing in the housing market.
Seiders said the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee likely will again raise short-term interest rates May 20 to try to curb demand-led growth in housing and other sectors.
The Fed boosted rates a quarter percentage point March 25.

Strong job and income gains have fostered high levels of consumer confidence, while stock market gains last year put more money in would-be homebuyers' pockets, delaying a slowdown in the housing sector.

"Basically, we see the second quarter staying very close to the first quarter, so there's not much chance of an abrupt weakening," Seiders said, especially since buyers have the option of turning to adjustable-rate mortgages as fixed rates go up with credit readily available.
The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. said rates for a 30-year mortgage loan averaged 7.90 percent in March, up from 7.65 percent in February and 7.62 percent in March 1996.

Joel Naroff, Philadelphia-based economist for First Union Corp. in Charlotte, N.C., said the recent faltering in stock prices may exert some drag on demand but in the meatime the housing sector was in such "incredibly good shape" during March that it was nearly inviting policy action to slow it.
"The Fed will take note of this strong number and recognize that it has to do more to slow down the economic freight train," Naroff predicted.
Sales of new homes in March were running at a brisk 14.3 percent above a year earlier, when they were selling at a rate of 711,000 a year, and inventories were lean.

There were 297,000 new homes for sale across the country in March, down from 307,000 in February. It was the smallest inventory of available new homes since April 1994, when there also were 297,000 on the market.
So far, the most obvious sign of a widely predicted slowing in housing has come in the figures for sales of previously lived-in homes rather than new ones.
Last Friday the National Association of Realtors said sales of existing, or used, homes fell 2.8 percent in March to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.11 million.
For new homes, the March sales increase was concentrated in the West, where sales jumped 17.7 percent to 246,000 -- the most vigorous sales rate since 262,000 in November 1993.

In the Midwest, new home sales rose 2.5 percent in March to 123,000 a year. But sales in the Northeast dropped 16.1 percent to 94,000 a year and in the South they declined 10.5 percent to an annual rate of 351,000.
The average home sales price in March rose to $171,500 from $169,900 in February while the median sales price was up to $142,500 from $141,000.
